title: Year three close
hookLine: a year of great questions, answered in many voices

lines: GENTLY. LIVE, THEN. LOVE IS THE PRACTICE.
WORK WELL, THEN REST. LET IT GO. SMALLER, AND GLAD.
cards: Gently. Live, then. Love is the practice.
Work well, then rest. Let it go. Smaller, and glad.
Those were the lines that closed each block this year, one for each great question: suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness, awe. Read them in a row and they sound almost like a life.
None of them answers the question it closed. Each is more like a way of carrying it. And that is where year three ends: not with a verdict, but with a way of holding what's still unsolved.

teach.b: First, many voices, kept apart. On suffering, the Buddha named suffering and its cause, Job argued, and Julian heard that all shall be well.

On death, the Gita spoke of worn clothes, the Gospels of resurrection, Socrates of two possibilities, without claiming to know which was true. They didn't agree, and this year never pretended they did.
Each answer stayed in its own home, in its own words. Second, two pictures from a letter. A few days ago, Rilke told a young poet to love the questions themselves.

In that same letter he gives two images for what those questions are like: locked rooms, and books written in a language you can't read yet. You don't break a locked door down, or force a foreign book to make sense.
You live near them. Perhaps, Rilke says, one day you'll find you've lived your way into an answer.

teach.h: LOVING A QUESTION, NOT SOLVING IT.
teach.b: Third, loving a question isn't the same as solving it. You keep a loved question near the way you keep a friend near: you return to it, notice it has changed, and don't need it to end.
Nachiketa loved his so much he turned down Death's gifts for it.

Fourth, a close, not a stop. Tomorrow a new year begins, and the questions come with you. A question carried into new company tends to sound different there, the way a familiar song does in a new room.
That's what this year was for: not a shelf of finished answers, but a handful of questions you know well enough to love.

how: Some people mark the end of a year of study by rereading their notes and choosing one question to carry into the next year, sitting with it quietly rather than trying to settle it.

games.q: the closing lines: tap the pairs.

s: year three ended by blending the traditions' answers into one
each answer stayed in its own home, in its own words; they didn't agree, and the year never pretended they did.
Rilke compared the young poet's questions to locked rooms and books in a language he couldn't read yet
you don't force them open; you live near them.
loving a question means you've stopped looking for an answer
it means keeping the question near and returning to it, without needing it to end.

games.q: you're sitting with the question you love most, and your mind starts building an answer to it. what do you do?
o: finish the answer, so the question can be closed.
set the answer down and come back to the question.
give up on the question: it's taking too long.
games.why: today's practice: set the answer down and come back. loving a question means keeping it near, without needing it to end.

practice: Look at the list you made two days ago, or let the year's questions pass by until one stays: the one you're most glad to still be asking.

Hold it lightly, the way you'd hold a warm cup, and when your mind starts building an answer, set the answer down and come back to the question. If you pray, carry it into prayer; if not, let it keep you company.

wordCard.voice: Rilke. The poet who told a young correspondent to love the questions themselves, the way this year's great questions stayed open with care. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: love the questions. You don't need an answer to keep one close. Year three, done.
